title_en: Grohe AG v. Zhejiang Jianlong Sanitary Ware Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of design patent
ruling_gist_en: The design features of the granted design patent reflect its innovative content that differs from the prior art, and also reflect the designer's creative contribution to the prior art. If the accused infringing design does not include all the design features that distinguish the granted design from the prior art, it can generally be presumed that the accused infringing design is not similar to the granted design patent.
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over infringement of design patent right; Retrial; Supreme People's Court; Zhejiang Province; Legal person; Foreign-invested enterprise; Patent Law; Determination of design features; Judgment of functional design features; Criteria for determining similarity of designs; Reversal of judgment; Design patent; Shower head; Patent infringement; Uniform adjudication standards; Clarify judicial yardstick; Patent right; Intellectual property; Dispute over infringement of design patent right
full_text_en:
Grohe AG v. Zhejiang Jianlong Sanitary Ware Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of design patent

[Ruling Summary]

The design features of an authorized design patent reflect its innovative content that distinguishes it from existing designs, and also embody the designer's creative contribution to existing designs. If the accused infringing design does not include all the design features that distinguish the authorized design from existing designs, it can generally be presumed that the accused infringing design is not similar to the authorized design.

For the determination of design features, the patentee shall provide evidence for the design features it claims, and a third party may provide rebuttal evidence to overturn them. On the basis of hearing the opinions of all parties on the evidence, the people's court shall fully examine the evidence and legally determine the design features of the authorized design.

The determination of functional design features does not depend on whether the design lacks alternatives due to functional or technical constraints, but on whether, from the perspective of an ordinary consumer of the design patent product, the design is solely determined by a specific function, without needing to consider whether the design has aesthetic appeal.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2015) Min Ti Zi No. 23

Re-Petitioner (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Zhejiang Jianlong Sanitary Ware Co., Ltd. Domicile: Qinggang Section, Yuhuan County Science and Technology Industrial Park, Zhejiang Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Cai Xianliang, Chairman of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zheng Caiwei, Attorney at Zhejiang Ivy Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Gu Wangjian, male, Han ethnicity, born on August 12, 1985, patent agent at Beijing Keyi Intellectual Property Agency (General Partnership), domiciled in Taizhou City, Zhejiang Province, People's Republic of China.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Grohe AG. Domicile: Filttermühle Platz 15, Düsseldorf, Federal Republic of Germany.

Litigation Representative: Rainer Mues, Vice President Finance of the Company.

Litigation Representative: Thomas Ziegler, Head of Legal and Patent Department of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Ke, Attorney at Beijing Wanhuida Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Rui, female, Han ethnicity, born on July 19, 1980, patent agent at Beijing Wanhuida Intellectual Property Agency Co., Ltd., domiciled in Fengtai District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

The re-petitioner Zhejiang Jianlong Sanitary Ware Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jianlong Company), due to a dispute with the respondent Grohe AG (hereinafter referred to as Grohe Company) over infringement of design patent rights, dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2013) Zhe Zhi Zhong Zi No. 255 rendered by the Higher People's Court of Zhejiang Province of the People's Republic of China, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court rendered the civil ruling (2014) Min Shen Zi No. 277 on December 18, 2014, granting the retrial of this case. After the retrial was granted, this Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and heard this case in open court on February 10, 2015. Attorney Zheng Caiwei appeared on behalf of Jianlong Company, and Attorneys Wang Ke and Wang Rui appeared on behalf of Grohe Company. This case is now concluded.

On November 29, 2012, Grohe Company filed a lawsuit with the Intermediate People's Court of Taizhou City, Zhejiang Province of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance), alleging that Jianlong Company's production, sale, and offer for sale of LYA series bathroom products of models GL062, S8008, etc., were identical or similar to its design patent product "Handheld Shower Head (NO.A4284410X2)" (Patent No. ZL200930193487.X), infringing its patent rights. Grohe Company requested the court to order Jianlong Company to: 1. Immediately cease the production, sale, and offer for sale of goods infringing the design patent right ZL200930193487.X; 2. Destroy the infringing products in stock and the molds specially used for producing the infringing products; 3. Compensate Grohe Company for economic losses of RMB 200,000, including reasonable expenses incurred by Grohe Company to stop the infringement; 4. Bear all litigation costs of this case.

The court of first instance found through trial: Grohe Company is a company established and existing under German law, with a business scope of research, development, manufacturing, and sale of sanitary ware fittings, accessories, and components, and trade in various products related to plumbing materials. On June 23, 2009, Grohe Company applied to the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as SIPO) for a design patent titled "Handheld Shower Head (NO.A4284410X2)", i.e., the patent in question, and was granted the patent on May 19, 2010, with the patent number ZL200930193487.X. The design patent is currently valid and legally effective.

Jianlong Company was established on April 15, 1998, with a registered capital of RMB 5,850,000, and its business scope includes manufacturing of sanitary ware, plumbing fittings, valves, metal accessories for construction and furniture, plastic crafts, lighting fixtures, electronic components for power, and import and export of goods and technology.

On September 19, 2012, Grohe Company commissioned Chai Yiling to apply to Yongxin Notary Public Office in Ningbo City, Zhejiang Province for evidence preservation notarization. The notary public office recorded that Jianlong Company was promoting a LYA series GL062 handheld shower product on its company website (website address: www.gllon.com) and issued the notarial certificate (2012) Zhe Yong Yong Zheng Min Zi No. 2298. On September 28 of the same year, Grohe Company commissioned a third party, Chen Yinghui, to apply for evidence preservation notarization at the Oriental Notary Public Office in Beijing. The notary personnel, together with the third party Mao Qingling, went to Jianlong Company located in Yuhuan Qinggang Science and Technology Industrial Park, Zhejiang Province, purchased ten shower heads from Jianlong Company's staff, obtained a receipt numbered 0024942, two brochures, and two business cards, and photographed and sealed the items obtained.

On December 3, 2012, based on Grohe Company's application for evidence preservation, staff from the court of first instance went to Jianlong Company and photographed the products in question identified by Grohe Company.

The shower head shown in the published drawings of the design patent in question includes two parts: a spray head and a handle. The spray head is a flat ellipse, appearing as a rounded rectangle from the front, with arc-shaped sides, smoothly tapering at the bottom to form an integrally connected handle. Relative to the handle, the spray head tilts forward. The front side of the spray head has a long elliptical area with outlet holes arranged radially. The lower end of the handle is cylindrical, gradually narrowing and flattening toward the connection with the spray head to form a flat ellipse. After comparison at the first instance trial, the similarities between Jianlong Company's accused infringing product and Grohe Company's design patent in question are as follows: Both are products of the same type. Overall, both consist of two parts: a spray head and a handle. The shape of the water outlet surface of the accused infringing product's head is the same as that of the patent in question, both showing outlet holes arranged radially in an area with rounded ends and a rectangular middle, with arc-shaped edges. The differences between the two are: 1. The periphery of the spray head of the accused infringing product is beveled, sloping from the back toward the water outlet surface, while the main view and left side view of the patent in question show the periphery of the spray head as an arc surface; 2. The water outlet surface of the accused infringing product's head is separated from the panel by only a single line, while the water outlet surface of the patent in question's head is separated from the panel by a band formed by two lines; 3. The distribution of outlet holes on the water outlet surface of the accused infringing product's head is slightly different from that of the patent in question; 4. The handle of the patent in question has a long elliptical switch design, which the accused infringing product does not have; 5. Although the connection between the head and handle of the patent in question has a certain bevel, the angle is very small, almost a straight-line connection, while the bevel angle produced by the connection between the head and handle of the accused infringing product is relatively large; 6. From the bottom view of the patent in question, the bottom of the handle is circular, while the bottom of the accused infringing product in the bottom view is a curved fan shape. The lower end of the handle of the patent in question is cylindrical, gradually narrowing and flattening toward the connection with the head to form a flat ellipse, while the lower end of the handle of the accused infringing product is a fan-shaped column, and the transition toward the spray head is also a fan-shaped column, with a curved protrusion in the middle section of the handle during the transition; 7. The bottom end of the handle of the accused infringing product has an arc-shaped decorative line connecting the bottom end of the handle with the back of the product, while the bottom end of the handle of the patent in question has no such design; 8. The length ratio between the head and handle of the patent in question differs from that of the accused infringing product, and the arc surface at the connection between the head and handle also differs.

The court of first instance held that one party to this case, Grohe Company, is a legal person under the Federal Republic of Germany, making this a foreign-related civil lawsuit. According to Article 21, Paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, "A civil lawsuit brought against a legal person or other organization shall be under the jurisdiction of the people's court in the place of the defendant's domicile," and Article 259, "For foreign-related civil lawsuits conducted within the territory of the People's Republic of China, the provisions of this Part shall apply. Where there are no provisions in this Part, other relevant provisions of this Law shall apply," and Article 146 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, "Compensation for damages arising from tortious acts shall be governed by the law of the place where the tortious act was committed," Jianlong Company manufactured and sold the accused infringing products at its company domicile, which is within the jurisdiction of the court of first instance. Both parties also agreed at the trial that the court of first instance should apply Chinese law to hear the infringement dispute, so the court of first instance has jurisdiction over this case and shall apply the laws of the People's Republic of China to hear this case.

The design patent in question is within its valid term and has a stable legal status, and should be protected by law. The focus of the dispute in this case is whether the accused infringing product produced, sold, and offered for sale by Jianlong Company is similar to the design patent in question and whether it infringes Grohe Company's design patent right. According to Article 10 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Patent Infringement Dispute Cases (hereinafter referred to as the Judicial Interpretation on Patent Infringement), "The people's court shall judge whether designs are identical or similar based on the knowledge level and cognitive ability of an ordinary consumer of the design patent product," and Article 11, "When determining whether designs are identical or similar, the people's court shall make a comprehensive judgment based on the overall visual effect of the design, taking into account the design features of the authorized design and the accused infringing design," combined with the comparison results at trial, although the patent in question and the accused infringing product are highly similar in the design of the water outlet surface of the spray head, there are differences in the peripheral design of the spray head, the separation method between the periphery of the spray head and the water outlet surface, the overall shape and detailed design of the handle, the connection method between the handle and the head, and the size and length ratio. Grohe Company argued that the design of the water outlet holes radially distributed in an area with rounded ends and a rectangular middle, with arc-shaped edges, is the design feature of the patent in question, and since the head design of the accused infringing product is identical to it, it should be deemed to infringe the design patent right. However, whether the design feature of Grohe Company's patent in question is the design of the water outlet surface of the spray head was not reflected in its brief description, and according to the knowledge level and cognitive ability of an ordinary consumer, a shower head product should include two main parts: a head and a handle. The respective design features of each part, as well as the connection method and proportion between them, are easily directly observed during use and form the basis of the overall visual effect of the shower head product, endowing it with design aesthetics. Therefore, it should be determined that the accused infringing product and the design patent in question have substantive differences in overall visual effect and are not similar. In summary, Jianlong Company's act of producing, selling, and offering for sale the accused infringing product did not infringe Grohe Company's patent right in question, and Grohe Company's claims did not comply with relevant legal provisions. The court of first instance did not support them. The court ruled: Reject Grohe Company's claims. The case acceptance fee of RMB 4,300 shall be borne by Grohe Company.

Grohe Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Higher People's Court of Zhejiang Province of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance).

The court of second instance also found that, based on Grohe Company's application, the court of first instance went to Jianlong Company on December 13, 2012, to preserve evidence. The date of preservation recorded in the first instance judgment was incorrect and should be corrected.

The court of second instance held that the focus of the dispute in this appeal was whether the design adopted by the accused infringing product fell within the scope of protection of Grohe Company's patent in question, and the civil liability that Jianlong Company might bear.

Article 59, Paragraph 2 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law) provides that the scope of protection of a design patent shall be based on the design of the product as shown in the drawings or photographs, and the brief description may be used to interpret the design of the product as shown in the drawings or photographs. Therefore, in a comparison for design infringement, it is generally inappropriate to compare the accused infringing product with the actual patented product, as factors such as the color configuration and gripping feel of the actual product, which are irrelevant to the comparison, may mislead the evaluating entity and affect the determination of infringement. Even if the patented product is made strictly according to the patent drawings, the comparison should still be made between the actual accused infringing product and the patent drawings to make a final judgment on infringement. In this case, after comparison, although the differences between the accused infringing design and the patented design as summarized in the first instance judgment generally exist, the infringement comparison is not simply a listing and accumulation of differences, but should strictly adhere to the principle of "overall observation, comprehensive judgment." In this regard, Article 11 of the Judicial Interpretation on Patent Infringement provides that when determining whether designs are identical or similar, the people's court shall make a comprehensive judgment based on the overall visual effect of the design, taking into account the design features of the authorized design and the accused infringing design. The design features of the authorized design that distinguish it from existing designs generally have a greater impact on the overall visual effect of the design compared to other design features of the authorized design. If there is no difference in overall visual effect between the accused infringing design and the authorized design, the people's court shall find them identical; if there is no substantive difference in overall visual effect, it shall find them similar. In this case, first, regarding the design features of the patent in question, the patent law applicable at the time of filing did not require a brief description to accompany the granted design patent text. A design feature that distinguishes a design from other designs and has a certain degree of recognition can be determined as its design feature, and the prerequisite for determining a design feature is not whether it is recorded in the brief description of the patent. With respect to the patent in question, Grohe Company clearly identified the track-shaped water outlet surface as the design feature and visual focal point of the patent, and this part is indeed the most recognizable design of the patent in question, occupying the main visual area and bringing a relatively unique design aesthetic. Moreover, during the trial, the court of second instance specifically required Jianlong Company to conduct further research to confirm whether there was any existing design with a track-shaped water outlet surface for a shower head before the filing date of the patent in question. Jianlong Company failed to provide any corresponding existing design for comparison. Therefore, the track-shaped water outlet surface design of the spray head in the patent in question should be considered a design feature distinguishing it from existing designs and given significant weight, and the accused infringing design precisely adopts a highly similar water outlet surface design, thereby possessing this design feature of the patent in question. Next, the accused infringing design is very similar to the patented design in the overall contour of the shower head, the length ratio between the head and the handle, and other aspects. Furthermore, the main difference between the accused infringing design and the patented design is that the former lacks a type of track-shaped push-button design on the handle present in the latter. Although the push button can have different shape designs, its placement on the handle is primarily based on functional design and does not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the product. As for the other differences summarized in the first instance judgment, such as the peripheral design of the spray head and the method of separation from the water outlet surface, the shape of the handle, and the connection method between the handle and the head, these differences are relatively minor and also fail to create a substantive difference in the overall visual effect between the accused infringing design and the patented design. In summary, the court of second instance found that the accused infringing design was similar to the patented design and fell within the scope of protection of the design patent in question. Since Jianlong Company did not dispute that it had engaged in the acts of manufacturing, offering for sale, and selling the accused infringing product, it should bear corresponding infringement liability.

Regarding the determination of infringement liability, according to Article 65 of the Patent Law, since neither the infringer's gains nor the right holder's losses could be proved, and no reasonable patent licensing fee was available for reference, this case adopted statutory damages to determine the amount of compensation. The court of second instance held that, taking into account that the patent in question is a design patent with a certain design aesthetic and a history of multiple judicial protections; Jianlong Company's registered capital is RMB 5,850,000, indicating a certain production scale and marketing capability; Jianlong Company engaged in manufacturing, offering for sale, and selling the accused infringing product; and Grohe Company incurred corresponding rights enforcement costs to stop the infringement, the amount of compensation was discretionarily determined to be RMB 100,000. Jianlong Company's inventory products should also be destroyed, and Grohe Company's claim in this regard was supported. However, since Grohe Company did not prove that Jianlong Company currently holds the molds for producing the accused infringing product, Grohe Company's claim to destroy the molds specially used for producing the accused infringing product was not supported. The court ruled: 1. Reverse the first instance judgment; 2. Jianlong Company shall immediately cease manufacturing, offering for sale, and selling products infringing the design patent in question, and destroy the infringing products in stock upon service of this judgment; 3. Jianlong Company shall compensate Grohe Company for economic losses (including reasonable expenses incurred by Grohe Company to stop the infringement) in the amount of RMB 100,000; 4. Reject Grohe Company's other claims. The case acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 4,300, shall be borne by Jianlong Company in the amount of RMB 3,225 each, and by Grohe Company in the amount of RMB 1,075 each.

Jianlong Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, filed an application for retrial with this Court, arguing: (1) The second-instance judgment was erroneous in its findings of material facts. 1. The second-instance court incorrectly summarized the design features and visual essential parts of the patent in question and erroneously found that the accused infringing design was highly similar thereto. First, the second-instance court determined that the design feature and visual essential part of the patent in question was its track-shaped water outlet surface, a design that had been disclosed by design patent No. 200630113512.5 prior to the filing date of the patent in question and thus constituted prior art. Shower head products consist of a head and a handle; the design features of these two parts, their connection, and their proportional dimensions are all readily observable during use, forming the basis for the overall visual effect of shower head products and endowing them with aesthetic design. The head of the shower head, however, is necessarily used for water outflow due to its function and generally does not attract particular consumer attention. The second-instance court, based solely on Grohe's one-sided statement, identified it as a design feature and visual essential part, which was contrary to common sense. Second, the second-instance court found that the accused infringing design adopted a water outlet surface design highly similar to that of the patent in question, thereby possessing that design feature of the patent. In fact, the patent in question has a track-shaped water outlet surface that is planar, whereas the accused infringing design employs an arc-shaped design with the water outlet surface not lying in the same plane as the arc. Arc-shaped designs are common in the design industry and cannot be monopolized by anyone; still less should the patent's planar track-shaped water outlet surface be conflated with the three-dimensional water outlet surface formed by arcs in the accused infringing design. 2. The second-instance court erroneously found that the accused infringing design was similar to the patent in question. Regarding the differences between the accused infringing design and the patent in question, the first-instance court comprehensively enumerated eight aspects of difference, including the shape of the handle, the peripheral design of the shower head, the division of the water outlet surface, and the connection between the handle and the head, differences sufficient for an ordinary consumer to quickly and clearly distinguish between the two. As a whole, shower head products are all composed of a handle and a water outlet surface; the length of the handle is based on the width of an average human palm, while the length and width of the water outlet surface are established based on the handle's length, and both should maintain an appropriate proportion to preserve basic aesthetics. The second-instance court found that "the accused infringing design and the design of the patent in question are very similar in terms of the overall contour of the shower head and the proportional division of the head and the handle," erroneously attributing the overall composition and proportional division of both entirely to the unique design of the patent in question. In fact, the two differ completely in overall contour and the proportional division of the head and handle. 3. The second-instance court erroneously summarized the main differences between the accused infringing design and the patent in question. As noted above, there are as many as eight aspects of difference between the two, but the second-instance court erroneously identified the main difference as the former lacking a track-shaped push-button design found on the handle of the latter. Moreover, the second-instance court's classification of the push button on the handle as a functional design was self-contradictory; if the push button were truly a functional design, the accused infringing design should also have a push button on its handle, yet in fact, the accused infringing design has no push button on the handle at all. (2) The second-instance court erred in its application of the law. In this case, the accused infringing design and the patent in question have substantial differences in overall visual effect and significant differences in detail; they are not similar. The second-instance court's judgment that Jianlong Company should bear liability for infringement damages to Grohe Company was erroneous. In summary, Jianlong Company applied for retrial pursuant to Articles 200(1), (2), and (6) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, requesting that this Court set aside the second-instance judgment, dismiss Grohe Company's claims, and order Grohe Company to bear the litigation costs of the first and second instances.

Grohe Company submitted its opinions, arguing: (1) The grounds for Jianlong Company's retrial application are untenable. 1. Jianlong Company conducted a strict and detailed comparison of the patent in question and the accused infringing design from a professional perspective, but for the ordinary consumer of shower head products, the differences found are minor and do not result in a substantial difference in the overall visual effect of the products. 2. The shower head product of design patent No. 200630113512.5 has a rectangular water outlet surface, which is neither identical nor similar to the patent in question; the water outlet surface design of the patent in question is not prior art. 3. The water outlet surfaces of both the patent in question and the accused infringing design feature water outlet holes arranged radially within an area with rounded ends and a rectangular middle, with arcuate edges; they are clearly highly similar. From the left side view of the patent in question, the water outlet surface is not planar either. (2) The accused infringing design falls within the scope of protection of the patent in question. 1. The design point of the patent in question is the water outlet surface, which is highly similar to that of the accused infringing design. The second-instance evidence submitted by Grohe Company and the patent search report for the patent in question can demonstrate that this design point has high novelty. 2. For ordinary consumers using shower heads, the water outlet part at the head of the shower head is readily observable during normal use; the handle portion is either held in hand or mounted on a bracket. In this case, the water outlet surface of the shower head has a greater impact on the overall visual effect of the appearance design compared to other parts, and it should be found that the accused infringing design and the patent in question are similar. (3) The design space for shower heads is substantial, so the standard for determining similarity should be relaxed.

During the retrial review stage of this case, Jianlong Company submitted the following evidence to this Court:

1. A copy of the first-instance trial transcript, intended to prove that Grohe Company had asserted during the first instance that the shower head, handle, and their connection were distinguishing design features of the patent in question.
2. A printed copy of the design patent view for shower head patent No. 200630113512.5 from the website of the State Intellectual Property Office, intended to prove that the "track-shaped water outlet surface" of the patent in question was prior art.
3. Copies of No. 17086 Invalidation Request Review Decision (hereinafter "Decision No. 17086") regarding the design patent in question and Grohe Company's statement of opinion during that invalidation proceeding, intended to prove that both Grohe Company and the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter "Patent Reexamination Board") considered that differences in the shower head, handle, and their connection could significantly affect the overall visual effect, allowing different designs to be distinguished.

After cross-examination, Grohe Company had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 1 submitted by Jianlong Company but disputed its relevance, arguing that the distinguishing design features claimed by Grohe Company included the shower head, handle, and connection, covering those asserted in the second instance, and that the emphasis on the distinguishing design features of the water outlet surface in the second instance did not deny the distinguishing design features mentioned in the first instance. Grohe had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 2 but disputed its relevance, arguing that the water outlet surface in evidence 2 was rectangular, rendering it neither identical nor similar to that of the patent in question. Grohe had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 3 but disputed its relevance, arguing that Grohe's statements regarding distinguishing features in the invalidation proceeding were not contradictory to its relevant statements in the second instance; they merely referenced different comparators, the former being a distinction from a single prior art design cited by the invalidation requester, the latter being derived from a comparison with 12 prior art designs submitted in the second instance.

During the retrial review stage of this case, Grohe Company submitted the following evidence to this Court:

1. Notarial certificate No. (2014) Jing Fang Yuan Nei Jing Zheng Zi No. 14124 issued by the Fangyuan Notary Public Office, Beijing, PRC, primarily containing screen captures of relevant webpages of Jianlong Company, intended to prove that Jianlong Company continued to manufacture and offer for sale the accused infringing product after the second-instance judgment.
2. Appearance design search report (No. GW10393) issued by the Patent Search and Advisory Center of the State Intellectual Property Office, intended to prove the high novelty of the patent in question.
3. A printed copy of the online receipt for the annual fee payment of the patent in question, intended to prove that the patent in question is legally valid.

After cross-examination, Jianlong Company had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 1 submitted by Grohe Company but disputed its relevance, arguing that the product images shown in the notarial certificate were neither identical nor similar to the patent in question. Jianlong had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 2 but disputed its relevance, arguing that a search report might miss patents identical or similar to the patent in question. Jianlong had no objection to the authenticity or legality of evidence 3 but disputed its relevance.

After review, this Court finds that the evidence submitted by Jianlong Company and Grohe Company has been verified; neither party has objected to the authenticity or legality of the other's evidence. Therefore, this Court confirms the above evidence. The issue of whether this evidence can prove the intended matters will be discussed in the reasoning section of this judgment.

This Court holds that the dispute in this case centers on whether the appearance design of the accused infringing product falls within the scope of protection of the design patent in question.

Article 59(2) of the Patent Law provides: "The scope of protection of a design patent right shall be determined by the design of the product as shown in the drawings or photographs. The brief description may be used to interpret the design of the product as shown in the drawings or photographs." Article 8 of the Judicial Interpretation on Patent Infringement provides: "If a design that is identical or similar to the granted design is used in a product of the same or a similar kind as the product of the design patent, the people's court shall find that the accused infringing design falls within the scope of protection of the design patent right provided in Article 59(2) of the Patent Law." Article 10 provides: "The people's court shall determine whether designs are identical or similar based on the knowledge level and cognitive ability of the ordinary consumer of the design patent product." In this case, the accused infringing product and the product of the design patent in question are the same, both being shower head products. Therefore, the key issue in this case is whether, for the ordinary consumer, the appearance design of the accused infringing product is identical or similar to the granted design in question. This involves the following four specific issues:

I. Regarding the design features of the granted design in question

This Court holds that the legislative purpose of the design patent system is to protect innovative industrial designs that have aesthetic appeal. A design must contain recognizable innovative features that distinguish it from prior designs to be granted a patent; these innovative features constitute the design features of the granted design. Generally, designers innovate based on prior designs. For products already on the market, a patented design usually contains some elements of prior designs as well as design elements that are neither identical nor similar to prior designs. It is precisely these elements that make the granted design innovative, thereby satisfying the substantive grant conditions set forth in Article 23 of the Patent Law: it is not prior art, there is no conflicting application, and it has an obvious distinction from prior designs or combinations of prior design features. The description of these elements constitutes the design features of the granted design, reflecting its innovative content different from prior designs and the designer's creative contribution to prior designs. Because of these design features, an ordinary consumer can easily distinguish the granted design from prior designs, and thus they have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the design product. If the accused infringing design does not include all the design features that distinguish the granted design from prior designs, it may generally be presumed that the accused infringing design is not similar to the granted design.

Regarding the determination of design features, generally, the patentee may record the design features in the brief description or may make corresponding statements regarding the design features during patent grant, confirmation, or infringement proceedings. According to the evidence rule "he who asserts must prove," the patentee bears the burden of proving the design features it claims. Additionally, the purpose of grant and confirmation proceedings is to examine the patentability of a design; therefore, relevant records in the examination documents of such proceedings have important reference value for determining design features. Ideally, the grant and confirmation of a design patent should be based on a complete search of all prior designs to identify a comparative design to assess patentability. However, due to limitations in search databases, the search capabilities of invalidation requesters, and other factors, the design features identified in the examination documents of grant and confirmation proceedings may not be derived from an exhaustive search of all prior designs. Therefore, whether the design features are proven by the patentee or determined based on records in the grant and confirmation examination documents, if a third party raises an objection, it should be allowed to submit counter-evidence to refute them. The people's court, after hearing the cross-examination opinions of all parties, shall fully examine the evidence and determine the design features of the granted design in accordance with the law.

In this case, the patentee Grohe Company claims that the track-shaped water outlet surface is a design feature of the granted design in question. Jianlong Company does not accept this. In this regard, this Court holds: First, the granted design in question has no brief description recording its design features. In the second-instance proceedings, Grohe Company submitted 12 design patent documents for shower head products, seven of which had a publication date earlier than the filing date of the patent in question. The designs shown in the accompanying drawings do not adopt a track-shaped water outlet surface. In the invalidation request review proceedings regarding the granted design in question, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Decision No. 17086, finding that compared with the closest comparative design, Evidence 1: "In terms of overall shape, compared with the previously disclosed design, the shape of the shower head and the transitions of its various surfaces, the design of the front water outlet area of the shower head, and the ratio of the shower head width to the handle diameter differ significantly. These differences are design contents that are easily noticed by the ordinary consumer." That is, the decision identified the shape of the shower head water outlet surface as one of the design features of the granted design in question. Second, although Jianlong Company does not accept that the track-shaped water outlet surface is a design feature of the granted design in question, it did not submit any corresponding evidence during the first or second instance to prove that the track-shaped water outlet surface was prior art. During the retrial review stage, Jianlong Company submitted a view of design patent No. 200630113512.5 for a shower head to prove that the track-shaped water outlet surface had been disclosed by prior art. Upon review, the publication date of that design patent is earlier than the filing date of the granted design in question, so it can serve as prior art for the granted design in question. However, its front view and usage state reference view show a water outlet surface with rectangular ends rather than arcuate ends; its water outlet surface is not track-shaped. Therefore, this Court does not support Jianlong Company's retrial ground that the track-shaped water outlet surface is not a design feature of the granted design in question.

II. Regarding the parts of the granted design product that are easily observable during normal use

Determining the parts of the granted design product that are easily observable during normal use should be based on the perspective of the ordinary consumer, considering the product's purpose and various usage states. In this case, first, the granted design in question is a shower head product design. A shower head product consists of a shower head and a handle, and the spatial proportions of these two parts in the overall product structure are relatively balanced. The shower head product can be handheld or wall-mounted. In its normal usage state, for the ordinary consumer, the shower head, handle, and their connection are all parts that are easily observable. Second, Decision No. 17086 found that the design of prior application Evidence 2 used the same track-shaped water outlet surface as the granted design in question. However, because "the shower head and handle of the granted design are integral, all surfaces of the shower head and its connection to the handle are arcuate, and the shower head is tilted forward, which differs significantly from the prior application design; the above differences are design contents easily noticed by the ordinary consumer," it found that the two designs were neither identical nor similar. Thus, the readily observable parts of a shower head product are not limited to the water outlet surface of the shower head head; when comprehensively assessing the overall visual effect of a shower head product's appearance design, the shower head, handle, and their connection should all be considered as parts that are easily observable.

III. Whether the push button on the handle of the granted design in question is a functional design feature

This Court holds that a functional design feature in appearance design refers to a feature that, from the perspective of the ordinary consumer of the design product, is solely determined by the specific function to be realized by the product, without considering aesthetic factors. Generally, designers consider both functional and aesthetic factors when designing a product's appearance. While realizing the product's function, improvements are made to the product's appearance in accordance with humanistic rules and principles. That is, the product must first fulfill its function, and second, it must be visually appealing. With respect to a particular feature of a design, in most cases it is both functional and decorative. The designer will choose a design that it considers most aesthetically pleasing from among multiple designs that can achieve the specific function. A design that is solely determined by a specific function exists only in rare, exceptional cases. Therefore, functional design features in appearance design include two types: one is the sole design for achieving a specific function; the other is one of several designs for achieving a specific function, but that design is determined solely by the specific function to be realized, without regard to aesthetic considerations. The key to determining a functional design feature is not whether the design is non-selectable due to functional or technical constraints, but whether, from the perspective of the ordinary consumer of the design product, the design is determined solely by the specific function, without considering whether the design has aesthetic appeal. Generally, functional design features do not have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of an appearance design; while design features that are both functional and decorative have an impact on the overall visual effect that needs to consider the strength of the decorative element: the stronger the decorative element, the greater the relative impact on the overall visual effect, and vice versa.

In this case, one of the differences between the granted design in question and the appearance design of the accused infringing product is that the latter lacks a type of track-shaped push-button design found on the handle of the former. The function of the push button is to control the water flow switch. Whether to include a push button component is determined by whether the function of controlling the water flow switch needs to be realized on the shower head product. However, as long as a push button is placed on the handle of the shower head, the shape of the push button can have multiple designs. When an ordinary consumer sees a push button on the handle of a shower head, they will naturally pay attention to its decorative quality and consider whether the push button design is aesthetically pleasing, rather than merely considering whether the push button can realize the function of controlling the water flow switch. The designer of the granted design in question chose to design the push button on the handle as track-shaped, with the purpose of coordinating with the track-shaped water outlet surface to enhance the overall aesthetic appeal of the product. Therefore, the second-instance judgment's determination that the push button in the granted design in question was a functional design feature constituted an error in the application of law, and this Court hereby corrects it.

4.  Regarding whether the design of the accused infringing product and the authorized design in question are identical or similar

Article 11 of the Judicial Interpretation on Patent Infringement provides that, when determining whether a design is identical or similar, a comprehensive judgment shall be made based on the overall visual effect of the design, taking into account the design features of the authorized design and the accused infringing design; design features that are primarily determined by technical functions shall not be considered. Parts that are easily observed directly during normal use of the product, compared to other parts, and design features of the authorized design that distinguish it from the prior design, compared to other design features of the authorized design, generally have a greater impact on the overall visual effect of the design.

In this case, compared with the authorized design in question, the design of the accused infringing product has its water outlet holes distributed within a track-shaped area on the front of the shower head. Although there are slight differences in the number of water outlet holes and their distribution at the two ends of the water outlet surface compared with the authorized design in question, overall, the accused infringing product adopts a track-shaped water outlet surface design that is highly similar to the authorized design in question. Regarding the distinguishing design features between the two, the court of first instance summarized eight aspects, which were not disputed by either party. As for these distinguishing design features: First, as mentioned above, Decision No. 17086 determined that the design features of the authorized design patent in question are threefold: (1) the shape of the shower head and the transition of its various surfaces; (2) the shape of the water outlet surface of the shower head; and (3) the ratio of the width of the shower head to the diameter of the handle. Apart from the design feature of the shape of the water outlet surface of the shower head, other design features such as the shape of the shower head and the transition of its various surfaces, and the ratio of the width of the shower head to the diameter of the handle also have a significant impact on the overall visual effect of the product. Although the design of the accused infringing product adopts a track-shaped water outlet surface highly similar to that of the authorized design in question, regarding the design feature of the shape of the shower head and the transition of its various surfaces, the shower head, handle, and their connecting surfaces of the authorized design in question all have arc transitions, while the shower head, handle, and their connecting surfaces of the design of the accused infringing product all have beveled transitions. This results in a clear difference in the overall design style between the two. Additionally, for the distinguishing design features between the design of the accused infringing product and the authorized design in question beyond the design features, as long as they are sufficient to cause a clear difference in the overall visual effect between the two, they should also be considered. Second, for a shower head product, the shower head, the handle, and the connection between them are all parts that are easily observed directly during normal use. When making a comprehensive judgment on the overall visual effect, the designs of these parts should be given focused consideration. Specifically, the handle of the authorized design in question is provided with a track-shaped push button, whereas the accused infringing product has no such design. Since this push button is not a functional design feature, the presence or absence of the push button, as a distinguishing design feature, will affect the overall visual effect of the product. The bevel angle formed at the connection between the shower head and the handle in the authorized design in question is relatively small, whereas the bevel angle formed at the connection between the shower head and the handle in the accused infringing product is relatively large, resulting in a clear difference in the left side view between the two. It is precisely because the design of the accused infringing product does not include all the design features of the authorized design in question, and because of the distinguishing design features of the design of the accused infringing product compared with the authorized design in question, such as the handle and the connection between the shower head and the handle, that the overall visual effects of the two are clearly different. The two are neither identical nor similar, and the design of the accused infringing product does not fall within the scope of protection of the design patent in question. The judgment of the second instance focused only on the design feature of the track-shaped water outlet surface of the authorized design in question, but did not consider other design features of the authorized design in question, nor the distinguishing design features between the design of the accused infringing product and the authorized design patent in question at other parts of the shower head product that are easily observed directly during normal use. It determined that the two were similar, which was an error in the application of law, and this Court corrects that error.

In summary, the design of the accused infringing product produced, offered for sale, and sold by Jianlong Company is neither identical nor similar to the authorized design in question owned by Grohe AG, and does not fall within the scope of protection of the authorized design patent. The acts of Jianlong Company in producing, offering for sale, and selling the accused infringing product do not constitute infringement of Grohe AG's patent rights in question. The judgment of the second instance contained an error in the application of law, and this Court shall correct it according to law. Pursuant to Article 59(2) of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 8, 10, and 11 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Patent Infringement Dispute Cases, and Article 207(1) and Article 170(1)(2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1.  The Civil Judgment (2013) Zhe Zhi Zhong Zi No. 255 of the Zhejiang High People's Court of the People's Republic of China is hereby vacated;

2.  The Civil Judgment (2012) Zhe Tai Zhi Min Chu Zi No. 573 of the Taizhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province of the People's Republic of China is hereby affirmed.

The case acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each RMB 4,300, shall be borne by Grohe AG.

This judgment is final.
